parsed.hook: Granite boulders the size of cars litter the vineyards of Cebreros, forcing Garnacha roots to tunnel deep for water in Spain’s continental interior. Comando G’s El Reventon leans on Alicante Henri Bouschet—an obscure, pigment-rich cross—to amplify the wine’s already inky depth, a choice that turns Sierra de Gredos’ granite minerality into something darker and more brooding than the region’s usual bright, floral Garnachas.
parsed.wine_summary: Comando G emerged from the Sierra de Gredos’ old-vine Garnacha revival, but El Reventon is their outlier: a table red that trades the appellation’s signature lift for a denser, almost Syrah-like darkness. The wine comes from 80-year-old Garnacha and a small parcel of Alicante Henri Bouschet, a grape bred in 1866 to add color and tannin to weak blends. Here, it does more—its anthocyanin-rich flesh (the same compound that stains your teeth) gives the wine a purple-black hue and a chewy, almost rustic edge that grounds the Garnacha’s red fruit. The producer’s biodynamic practices (certified since 2015) and 14-month oak aging in used barrels (mostly 500L) are less about flavor addition and more about textural integration, letting the granite’s sharp minerality cut through the wine’s natural richness.
parsed.terroir_expression: Cebreros sits on the southern flank of the Sierra de Gredos, where the Central System’s granite batholiths—formed 300 million years ago—erode into coarse, sandy soils laced with quartz and feldspar. This is continental climate territory: hot, dry summers (up to 40°C in July) and cold winters (down to -10°C), with a 1,000-meter altitude that tempers the heat and extends the growing season. The granite’s low fertility forces vines to dig deep, concentrating flavors and tightening tannins. In El Reventon, this translates to a wine that’s both dense and linear—blackberry and plum fruit wrapped in a stony, almost ferrous grip. The Alicante Henri Bouschet, planted in the rockiest parcels, amplifies the effect, its thick skins and pigmented flesh adding a layer of dark, earthy complexity that’s rare in Gredos.
parsed.vinification_summary: Comando G ferments El Reventon in open-top concrete vats with native yeasts, a choice that preserves the wine’s wild, savory edge. The Alicante Henri Bouschet (about 15% of the blend) is co-fermented with Garnacha, a technique that softens the former’s rustic tannins while deepening the latter’s color. After 30 days of maceration—long for Garnacha, which typically sees 10-15—the wine is racked into used oak barrels (mostly 500L, some 225L) for 14 months. The larger format minimizes oak influence, letting the granite’s minerality and the Alicante’s dark fruit take center stage. *Carbonic maceration* isn’t used here, but the extended skin contact achieves a similar effect: smoother tannins without sacrificing structure. The result is a wine that’s both bold and polished, with the Alicante’s inky depth and the Garnacha’s brightness in tension.

It’s worth it if you want a Gredos Garnacha with added depth and rustic complexity, but skip if you prefer the region’s brighter, more floral styles. It’s also a collector’s item, with allocations selling out quickly at specialty retailers like Astor Wines and Les Caves de Pyrene. parsed.insider_take: Most people assume El Reventon is just another Gredos Garnacha, but the Alicante Henri Bouschet changes everything. It’s not a wine for fans of bright, floral styles—this is for drinkers who want something darker, chewier, and more brooding. The tradeoff? It’s less versatile at the table than Comando G’s other wines (e.g., Rumbo al Norte), but it’s one of the few Spanish reds that can stand up to big, fatty dishes without oak sweetness. If you love Bandol or Cornas, this is your Gredos answer.
